1 Introduction
The ﬁeld of computational ﬂuid dynamics (CFD) is rapidly expanding its frontiers, opening new opportunities
to investigate ﬂow problems of unprecedented complexity and realism. It is therefore a great pleasure to
introduce this Collection of Acta Mechanica, entitled “Advanced CFD Modeling for Real-world Internal and
External Fluid Dynamics Problems.” The guiding idea behind this group of papers is to bring advanced
computational methods closer to practical applications, showing how state-of-the-art CFD can provide not
only deeper physical insight but also more reliable predictions for some of today’s most challenging ﬂow
scenarios in engineering.
Over the past decade, I have personally witnessed a remarkable transformation in CFD. Problems that once
required heavy simpliﬁcations or idealized geometries can now be tackled with high-ﬁdelity direct numerical
simulations (DNS), sophisticated reduced-order models (ROMs), or multi-physics couplings able to account
for thermal, chemical, or particulate effects. These advances are not conﬁned to academic laboratories; they
resonate strongly within the broader international community, where the interplay between CFD, artiﬁcial
intelligence (AI), and high-performance computing (HPC) is shaping the next generation of research.
Recent international events provide vivid evidence of this trend. The 1st International Symposium on AI
and Fluid Mechanics (AIFLUIDs 2025) [1], held in Chania, Greece, gathered more than 300 participants
from 34 countries, testifying to the global momentum of AI-driven approaches for analyzing and controlling
complexﬂows.Inthesamespirit,theEUROMECH–ERCOFTACColloquiumonData-DrivenFluidMechanics
(London, 2025) [2] brought together specialists in turbulence, machine learning, and uncertainty quantiﬁcation
to demonstrate how data-driven algorithms, when coupled with exascale computational resources, can be
integrated with traditional CFD tools to address problems once thought intractable.
High-performance computing remains a cornerstone of this evolution. Dedicated meetings such as the
Parallel CFD (ParCFD) conference series [3] now include sessions explicitly focused on the convergence of
AI and exascale simulation, illustrating how HPC resources are being leveraged for massively parallel ﬂow
solvers. Broader HPC venues reinforce this message: at the Supercomputing 2024 (SC24) conference [4],
live demonstrations of GPU-accelerated clusters showcased how industrial solvers like Ansys Fluent and
open-source codes can achieve unprecedented performance in cloud-based environments.
Even the largest gatherings in ﬂuid mechanics are now embracing these innovations. The APS Division
of Fluid Dynamics Annual Meeting, which attracts more than 3,500 participants each year, has introduced
entire sessions dedicated to machine learning, data-driven modeling, and physics-informed neural networks.
Similarly, the International Conference on Computational Fluid Dynamics (ICCFD) and the ECCOMAS
Congresses have placed increasing emphasis on AI-assisted turbulence modeling and exascale-ready CFD.

The long-standing ERCOFTAC workshops also reﬂect this evolution: the Direct and Large Eddy Simula-
tion (DLES) symposia remain a premier venue for presenting advances in high-ﬁdelity turbulence simulations,
with an increasing emphasis on bridging fundamental research with practical applications, while the Engineer-
ing Turbulence Modelling and Measurements (ETMM) conference series continues to connect fundamental
modeling approaches with a steadily broader range of applied engineering problems. In parallel, traditional
ﬂagship events for the engineering community such as the ASME Turbo Expo, the AIAA SciTech Forum,
and the AIAA Aviation Forum are increasingly hosting dedicated sessions on HPC acceleration, digital twins,
and multi-ﬁdelity modeling. These conferences highlight how CFD is being integrated into the design and
optimization pipelines of aerospace and turbomachinery industries, ensuring that advanced methods are trans-
lated into practical engineering impact. Taken together, these diverse events illustrate a global commitment
to coupling state-of-the-art CFD with emerging AI methodologies and to harnessing the full power of HPC.
This integration is paving the way toward more predictive, scalable, and efﬁcient solutions for some of today’s
most demanding real-world ﬂuid dynamics challenges.
Thus, in assembling this Collection, my goal has been to highlight representative examples of how these
advances are being applied to address both internal and external ﬂows of engineering relevance. I am conﬁdent
that the ﬁve contributions presented here reﬂect not only the diversity of current efforts but also the cutting-edge
character of modern applied CFD research.
2 Authors’ collected contributions
The ﬁrst contribution, “Effects of surface imperfections on the boundary layer stability in a high speed ﬂow”
by Gong et al., tackles a fundamental question in high-speed aerodynamics: how small surface irregularities
can inﬂuence the balance between laminar and turbulent ﬂow. Through direct numerical simulations (DNS)
combined with linear stability theory (LST), the authors examine a Mach 4.5 boundary layer over a ﬂat plate
perturbed by backward-facing steps and microgrooves. Their results reveal that when these imperfections are
placeddownstreamofthesynchronizationpointofthesecond-modeinstability,theycanactuallydelaytheonset
of turbulence by attenuating unstable waves. Among the tested conﬁgurations, backward-facing steps proved
more effective than microgrooves in stabilizing the ﬂow. These ﬁndings open new perspectives on passive
ﬂow control strategies for supersonic vehicles, where maintaining laminar conditions directly translates into
reduced drag and improved efﬁciency.
The second paper, “Enhancing non-intrusive reduced-order models with space-dependent aggregation
methods” by Ivagnes et al., brings the discussion into the realm of data-driven modeling. Here the authors
introduce a mixed-ROM framework that blends several reduced-order models (ROMs) built using different
techniques—ranging from proper orthogonal decomposition to machine learning autoencoders—and combines
them with diverse interpolation strategies. By assigning spatially varying weights and predicting them with
a machine learning algorithm, the mixed-ROM adaptively selects the most accurate local model across the
domain. The methodology is validated on canonical aerodynamic cases, including airfoil ﬂows at different
Reynolds numbers and angles of attack. Results show that the aggregated model consistently outperforms
any individual ROM, while also providing a measure of predictive uncertainty. This work illustrates how
hybrid, data-driven approaches are becoming essential tools in CFD, extending the reach of surrogate models
to complex and variable ﬂow conditions without sacriﬁcing efﬁciency.
Shifting from external aerodynamics to combustion, the third contribution, “Analysis of effects of inlet air
and fuel conditions on reactive ﬂow characteristics in a gas turbine model combustion chamber” by Abedinejad
et al., addresses the physics of reacting two-phase ﬂows. Using an Eulerian–Lagrangian CFD framework
enriched with a steady ﬂamelet combustion model, radiation modeling, and a post-processing NOx prediction,
the study explores how variations in inlet air and fuel spray conditions affect ﬂame dynamics and pollutant
emissions. The ﬁndings are highly relevant for practical operation: higher spray velocities enhance mixing and
ﬂame temperature but also increase NOx emissions, while narrower spray cone angles lead to cooler ﬂames
and reduced pollutants. Similarly, elevated inlet air pressure intensiﬁes near-injector burning and raises NOx
levels, while increasing inlet air temperature has a limited effect until a critical threshold is reached. Together,
these results offer a detailed map of how injection strategies and boundary conditions can be tuned to optimize
both efﬁciency and emissions in gas turbine combustors.
The fourth article, “Extending the CFD-DEM coupling algorithm to accurately predict the particle separa-
tion in a two-phase air–solid particle ﬂow through an aerofall Autogenous Grinding (AG) mill” by Darbandi
et al., turns attention to industrial applications where multiphase physics dominate. The authors extend the

CFD–DEM (Discrete Element Method) coupling approach to capture the complex interaction between airﬂow
and granular material in an aerofall autogenous grinding mill. Unlike most prior work, which has focused on
slurry systems, this study emphasizes the role of air in dry particle separation. Validation against laboratory-
scale experiments conﬁrms the accuracy of the extended algorithm in predicting both overall particle motion
and individual trajectories. The validated model is then applied to a full-scale mill, identifying operating
conditions that maximize separation efﬁciency and minimize energy consumption. This work exempliﬁes
how advanced coupled simulations can inform the optimization of large-scale industrial equipment, where
predictive CFD-DEM tools can directly support improved design and performance.
The ﬁfth and ﬁnal paper, “Numerical characterisation of outboard dynamic-inlet waterjets: propulsive
aspects of intake/pump integration” by Avanzi et al., explores an innovative concept in marine propulsion: the
outboard dynamic-inlet waterjet (ODW). This design integrates an axisymmetric hydrodynamic intake nacelle
with an axial-ﬂow pump, enabling system-level evaluation independent of a speciﬁc vessel. Using Reynolds-
averaged Navier–Stokes simulations closed with the k–ω SST turbulence model and a cavitation model, the
study maps performance across a range of speeds and pump operating conditions. The analysis shows that
the ODW can achieve efﬁciencies comparable to the isolated pump under design conditions, while off-design
regimes reveal potential cavitation and choking near the diffuser throat that could compromise performance.
By examining these complex interactions entirely in silico, the paper contributes valuable insight into how
future waterjet systems might be optimized to avoid cavitation while maintaining high efﬁciency.
3 Conclusive remarks
In closing, the papers in this Collection underscore several prevailing trends in advanced CFD research. We
see the continued push for high-ﬁdelity physics-based simulation alongside the rise of data-driven model-
ing techniques. The integration of CFD with other computational methods and with multi-physics aspects is
expanding the scope of problems we can address. These developments are driven by both increasing compu-
tational power and a growing recognition of CFD’s role in practical engineering decision-making. As we look
ahead, I believe that CFD will become even more entwined with machine learning and optimization, enabling
faster turnaround from simulation to design, while still demanding rigorous validation against experiments
or higher-ﬁdelity computations. The works presented here demonstrate how advanced CFD modeling, when
applied with care and creativity, can yield not only scientiﬁc understanding but also tangible improvements in
engineering systems.
Finally, I would like to express my sincere gratitude to all the authors who contributed their outstanding
research to this Collection. I am also deeply thankful to the expert reviewers, whose thorough evaluations and
feedback have helped maintain the high quality of these publications. My appreciation extends to the editorial
team of Acta Mechanica for their support and guidance throughout the process. It has been a privilege to serve
as the guest editor for this Collection. I hope that readers ﬁnd these articles as insightful and inspiring as I do,
and that the advances reported here will stimulate further developments in CFD modeling for both fundamental
and applied ﬂuid dynamics challenges.
